When I first read this article there was something about it that bugged me. The concept is simple enough. If the stratosphere weren’t hot enough ir measurements wouldn’t present as they do because the part of the spectrum due to higher energy transitions at lower heights would be absorbed by colder gas further up. I went to the original article at the NASA site, and it is a bit more informative, but there was still that little lingering doubt. Then the light bulbs went on between the ears. These results aren’t any proof of a simple linear increase of temperature with altitude. An atmosphere doesn’t have to behave in a linear fashion. It can be layered with areas of alternating higher and lower temperature. Here’s a wiki titled ‘Atmospheric Temperature’ from our own planet. The relevant part is the chart on the upper left. As you can see the temperature first decreases with altitude, then increases again, followed by a further dip and ending with an apparent increase once more at the higher region of the graph (90 to 100 kms). An atmosphere can be more of a layer cake, and is in our case, as opposed to a simple ladder up and down. A snake in the old game of snakes and ladders.

So my unease was quieted. This article and even the one at NASA it was modelled on present an oversimplified picture of uniform increase (or decrease) in temperature that is different from the one truly studied system, our own.
